3–5 MINUTES · EVIDENCE CHALLENGE

Cell Detective: Observe First, Identify Second

Choose one complete cell in the middle or lower-middle of the photograph. Describe its outline, its neighbors, and any darker feature inside. Use shapes and positions, not organelle names yet.

There is no prize for the most confident guess. Useful observations and honest uncertainty are what count.

1 · Observe

Tap the photo to mark your chosen cell, or describe its location below. The marker records your selection; it does not identify anything.

No cell marked yet.

The image is blurry and unstained. It may not supply enough evidence for every answer.

2 · Choose → justify → reveal

For each question, choose an interpretation, record one visual clue, and set your confidence. “Insufficient evidence” is always a valid response. Feedback appears only when you submit that question.

0 of 3 responses submitted.

Question 1

Trace the shared outline between two neighboring compartments. What structure best explains it, and what does the overall pattern suggest: plant peel tissue, loose animal cells, or insufficient evidence? Can you prove this is onion from this picture alone?

Question 2

Look for darker round or oval spots inside several compartments. What could they be, and does this photograph resolve a nucleolus inside a nucleus?

Question 3

What can the pale interior of a complete cell and the overall blue-green tint tell you about a central vacuole and chloroplasts? Distinguish a visible feature from an inference.

3 · Connect the evidence

Teaching notes stay hidden until you submit all three responses or explicitly request them.

Observe before naming. This photo shows closely packed, elongated polygonal compartments with darker outlines and small darker dots in many compartments. The broad pale region to the right is beyond the tissue edge: do not mistake it for the interior of your selected cell.

Build a cautious identification. Shared boundaries and the packed pattern support plant epidermal peel tissue. Onion bulb epidermis is plausible, not species-level proof. Neither exact magnification nor stain identity can be established from the photograph alone.

Separate visible features from interpretations. The boundary network is consistent with cell walls—a cell structure, not an organelle. Repeated intracellular round or oval dark spots are likely nuclei; one isolated dot could be an artifact. Do not call a dot a nucleolus when a surrounding nucleus is not resolved.

Respect the limits. A pale central cell interior is compatible with a central vacuole, but its membrane is not clearly resolved. The plasma membrane and thin cytoplasmic layer are not separately identifiable here. Mitochondria, ribosomes, and nucleoli are not required visible answers.

Color is not identification. A uniform blue-green tint is not evidence of chloroplasts. Identifying chloroplasts requires discrete bodies; none are clearly resolved here.

If you are also using a live microscope, a gentle fine-focus adjustment may help you check a boundary or spot. This is optional and cannot change the static photograph.

Source basis: Millersville’s onion microscopy laboratory identifies shared partitions as cell walls. Ohio State’s microscopy examples show stained onion nuclei at 100×, nucleoli in a separate 1000× view, and discrete green chloroplasts in Elodea. Those magnifications and staining conditions describe the reference examples, not your photo. The Jones & Bartlett laboratory text distinguishes the wall from the unresolved plasma membrane and infers vacuole position from the light central area.

Finish · Sketch your evidence

On paper, sketch your chosen cell and one neighbor. Keep the sketch simple:

  • Label one shared boundary cell wall.
  • If you saw a convincing intracellular spot, mark it likely nucleus ?. Otherwise write “not resolved.”
  • Mark the pale central area central vacuole — inferred, membrane not resolved.

Carry your uncertainty into the sketch. A careful “not enough evidence” is better than adding a structure you did not see.
